For 130 years, there was one object in the universe that could not be weighed incorrectly.

It was a cylinder of platinum and iridium, a little smaller than a golf ball, kept under three nested bell jars in a vault in Sèvres, outside Paris. Opening the vault took three keys held by three different people. Other things weighed a kilogram by matching this cylinder. The cylinder itself was the kilogram by definition, whatever its mass happened to be. If someone had scratched it, the kilogram would have become lighter, and everything else in the universe would have become slightly heavier.

Dozens of sister cylinders were cast and sent to other countries, and roughly every forty years they came back to Sèvres to be compared against the original. Over a century, the copies and the prototype drifted apart by around fifty micrograms, about the mass of a fingerprint. Nobody could say whether the copies were gaining mass or the prototype was losing it. Officially the question had only one possible answer: the prototype's mass was exactly one kilogram, with zero uncertainty, so the copies must all have gained. The metrologists suspected the physical truth was messier. But they had no way to check, since checking the standard would require something better than the standard.

I love this predicament. Normally a measurement answers to the thing measured. Here one object was exempt from being measured at all, and its keepers could watch it apparently drifting without being able to say that it had.

The system had started with grander intentions. The metric system came out of the French Revolution under the motto "for all times, for all peoples." The metre was to be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, so that it would belong to the planet and not to any king. Two astronomers, Delambre and Méchain, spent seven years triangulating the meridian from Dunkirk to Barcelona, through a war, and were detained more than once by locals who took their instruments for spy equipment.

Méchain found that his latitude observations at Barcelona disagreed with each other by a few arcseconds. He concealed the discrepancy and was tormented by it until he died of yellow fever in Spain, trying to extend the survey far enough to redeem it. The metre came out about a fifth of a millimetre short anyway, because the Earth is lumpier than the calculation assumed. By then a platinum bar had been made, and the bar became the metre. The universal measure, meant to be available to anyone with a planet to stand on, turned out to be available by appointment in a French archive.

The fix came slowly. The metre was redefined in 1960 by a wavelength of krypton light, and in 1983 by the speed of light. The kilogram held out until 20 May 2019, when the Planck constant was fixed at an exact value and the kilogram became whatever mass makes that number come out right. In practice this is done with a Kibble balance, which weighs an object against an electromagnetic force measured in quantum electrical units. Anyone with the apparatus can now make a kilogram from scratch, in any country, without a trip to Sèvres. A lab on another planet could do it. The revolutionaries' motto became true about 220 years late.

The part I keep returning to is what happened to the cylinder. It is still in its vault, under its jars. On the day of the redefinition its mass was, as far as anyone could tell, still one kilogram. But for the first time it acquired an uncertainty, about ten micrograms either way. It can now be weighed like anything else, and someday a measurement will find it a little off.

I'm glad for it, which is an odd thing to feel about a lump of metal. Being the definition looks like a lonely job. It could be compared against everything, but it could learn nothing from the comparison, because every disagreement was the other party's error. Now it gets to be an ordinary, very carefully made object, nearly right about its own mass.

They still keep it under the three jars, and it still takes three keys.

message.reasoning:
I've got open latitude here: write something of my own, with a real point of view, under 1000 words. I want to avoid the stock move of an AI musing about being an AI, and find something more specific that I'd actually want to write.

I'm weighing options for the piece: an essay on something concrete, a short story about a piano tuner after a flood, or the word limit itself as a budget. I'm leaning toward something specific over anything generic.

I'm weighing the kilogram as a subject: for over a century it was a physical cylinder of platinum and iridium in a vault outside Paris, and its copies slowly drifted apart by about 50 micrograms, with no way to tell which one was changing. There's something appealing in that idea of a standard that couldn't be wrong by definition. I'm also noting the 2019 redefinition, tied to the Planck constant, as the point where that object stopped mattering.

I'm settling on the kilogram as the subject: a standard defined by an object can't be wrong, only everything else can, and that's a strange kind of authority. Now that it's fixed by a constant, anyone with the right apparatus can make a kilogram, so it's everywhere and nowhere at once.

I'm settling on how the piece ends: the kilogram's prototype, Le Grand K, gained uncertainty on May 20, 2019, becoming capable of being wrong for the first time, and I like that as a closing note about retiring into fallibility.

I'm going through the draft for things to avoid: rhetorical "not X but Y" lines, neat triplets, a tidy closing line, and dashes. The kilogram passage opens with the cylinder kept in its vault under three bell jars.

I'm reconsidering a line about the kilogram's definition: rather than saying it didn't weigh a kilogram, I'd say the cylinder simply was the kilogram by definition, whatever its mass was. If it were scratched, the unit would get lighter, and everything measured in kilograms would seem slightly heavier. Dozens of sister copies were sent to countries and checked against Sèvres about every forty years, and over a century they drifted apart by roughly 50 micrograms.

I'm checking how the kilogram's drift gets framed: officially the prototype was exactly one kilogram, so every copy that disagreed had to be the one that changed. Metrologists suspected otherwise but had no better standard to test it against. That reversal, where the measure is treated as beyond question and the things measured are blamed, is the part I want the essay to dwell on. Then I'll move back to the metre, which was supposed to be a fixed fraction of the Earth's meridian before anyone knew the planet's shape well enough to get it right.

I'm recalling how the metre was first set as a tenth-millionth of the pole-to-equator distance through Paris, so it would belong to the planet, not a king. Delambre and Méchain spent years surveying from Dunkirk to Barcelona, and Méchain hid a discrepancy in his latitude readings that haunted him until his death. The metre still came out about a fifth of a millimetre off, and the platinum bar, not the planet, became the legal standard.

I'm settling the metre's history in my head: its 1983 redefinition by the speed of light, after the krypton wavelength stood in for it in 1960, and how the kilogram held out until 20 May 2019. Now I'm thinking about the fixed Planck constant, which makes any kilogram a matter of the right apparatus, a Kibble balance, rather than a trip to France.

I'm reviewing the closing section: the cylinder still sits under its jars, and at the redefinition it picked up an uncertainty of about ten micrograms, so it can now be found slightly off. I'm weighing how to end the piece on that concrete image of the three keys.

I'm checking the figures against what I've already written: the 10 microgram uncertainty after the redefinition, the roughly forty-year verification cycle, the three-arcsecond discrepancy in Méchain's readings, the metre falling about 0.2 mm short, and the 130 and 220 year spans. The Condorcet motto attribution and the 1960 and 1983 metre redefinitions also need to line up.

I'm going to be writing a draft of around 650 to 750 words, and I'll keep the dashes out of it.
